title: 四级篇章听力：钟、步行与书信
instruction: 听完整一节3篇短文及各段后读出的问题，依次选择最佳答案。音频中材料和问题各读一遍，卷面只印四个选项。本原创使用节内编号1—10，各段对应1—3、4—6、7—10题。播放器可回听，正式单次听辨条件未强制。
audio_introduction: Section C. You will hear three passages. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D.
source_form_notice: 四级形式参照2024年12月第一套转载Section C：3段、3/3/4共10回应、每题四选；原创采用节内编号，问题只在录音与作者区。全部自有虚构内容及本机合成试听，非原考试原声；未独立教研/听辨/学生难度或产品等值验证。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: At the fictional Fern Lane Museum, a wall clock used to be described as the oldest object in the building. The description had been copied from an early guidebook and repeated for years. When a volunteer found a purchase receipt, she noticed that the date was much later than the label suggested. The museum did not immediately replace one confident date with another. A clock can contain parts made at different times, and the receipt might record a sale rather than the date of manufacture. The volunteer photographed the receipt and asked a specialist to examine the clock. The resulting label explained what the museum knew about the purchase and which questions remained unanswered. Some visitors missed the simple claim that it was the oldest object. Others said the new account helped them see why dating an object could be difficult. The museum kept the earlier label in its working file instead of destroying it. That way, a future researcher could trace how the description had changed. The volunteer says the most useful discovery was not merely a different date. It was the need to keep the reason for a label available, so that repetition alone would not gradually turn an uncertain statement into an unquestioned fact.

questions.spoken_question: What made the volunteer question the clock’s label?
options: A visitor had broken the clock.
A purchase receipt showed a later date.
The museum had moved to a newer building.
The guidebook had lost its cover.
questions.rationale: B购买凭证日期较晚；A未坏，C未迁，D书封无关。

questions.spoken_question: Why was the receipt not treated as a certain manufacturing date?
options: The volunteer was not allowed to photograph it.
The receipt named a different museum.
The clock had no moving parts.
A sale date need not be the date the clock was made.
questions.rationale: D买卖不等制造且零件可异时；A已拍，B无异馆，C没有无部件事实。

questions.spoken_question: Why did the museum retain the earlier label?
options: To let later researchers follow changes in its description.
To keep displaying the old claim as certain.
To avoid making a file of supporting evidence.
To sell copies of the early guidebook.
questions.rationale: A存workingfile供tracechange；B新标签说明不确定，C正保据，D无出售。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: A fictional company offered its staff a choice of lunchtime activities. One option was a short walk led by a volunteer. At first, the organiser measured its success by counting how many people joined. The number increased, but several regular walkers quietly stopped coming. When the organiser asked them why, their answers were practical. The group had begun walking faster in order to return on time, and conversation was becoming difficult for people at the back. The organiser shortened the route instead of asking those people to hurry. She also introduced a pause at one clear meeting point, so nobody had to keep talking while trying to catch up. Attendance did not immediately rise again. However, some former participants returned, and the group could finish within the lunch break at a pace they found comfortable. The organiser kept the attendance count, but stopped treating it as a complete description of the activity. She now asked for comments about the route and pace as well. The change was not presented as medical evidence that walking had improved staff health. It was a response to what this particular group said was preventing them from taking part. A simple count had been useful, but it had not explained the experience behind the number.

questions.spoken_question: What did the organiser initially use to judge the walk?
options: The length of the company’s history.
Medical tests after each lunch break.
questions.rationale: C起初只数参加人数；B明确非medicalevidence，A/D无。

questions.spoken_question: Why did some regular walkers stop joining?
options: The group’s faster pace made participation uncomfortable.
The activity had moved to the evening.
Staff were required to bring expensive equipment.
questions.rationale: A加快后后排跟难说难；B仍午间，C非禁止谈，D无设备费。

questions.spoken_question: What change did the organiser make?
options: She lengthened the route to attract faster walkers.
She replaced all comments with medical data.
She removed the lunch-break finishing time.
She shortened the route and added a meeting pause.
questions.rationale: D短路线+meetingpointpause；A反，B加comments非替掉，C仍限午休。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: When fictional college student Ella moved into a shared house, she found a box of letters addressed to a former resident. They had arrived after he left, and no forwarding address was written on them. Ella first planned to throw them away because most appeared to be advertisements. A housemate suggested checking with the landlord before deciding. The landlord could not give Ella the resident's private address, but agreed to contact him and ask what he wanted done. Two days later, the former resident replied through the landlord. Most envelopes could be recycled, but he was waiting for one letter about a course application. He described the sender and asked whether such an envelope was in the box. Ella found it unopened. Rather than send a photograph of its contents, she arranged to leave the sealed envelope at the letting office, where the resident would collect it. Afterwards, the housemates put a small tray near the door for letters sent to people who no longer lived there. A note explained that the landlord should be contacted before anything was discarded. They did not make a list of former residents' private addresses. The tray gave them a temporary place to keep the letters and a clear next step. It did not turn the current tenants into managers of somebody else's correspondence. Ella was glad she had asked before treating the whole box as rubbish.

questions.spoken_question: Why did Ella originally consider discarding the letters?
options: The landlord had told her they were all worthless.
Every envelope had already been opened.
The former resident had refused all contact.
questions.rationale: B大多似广告使她初想丢；A未告，C unopened，D后回应。

options: By publishing the resident’s private address.
By opening the course letter for Ella.
By contacting the former resident about his wishes.
By asking Ella to pay the course fee.
questions.rationale: C联系询意愿，A明确不提供地址，B不开信，D无付费。

questions.spoken_question: What did Ella do with the important letter?
options: She left it sealed at the letting office for collection.
She photographed its contents for all the housemates.
She threw it away with the advertisements.
She changed the name on the envelope.

questions.spoken_question: What was the purpose of the new tray?
options: To store a public list of private forwarding addresses.
To collect payments for former residents.
To replace every tenant’s personal letterbox.
To hold misdirected letters while the landlord was consulted.
questions.rationale: D暂放并contactlandlord；A不列地址，B无收款，C不替个人信箱。
